profiles.meeting_scenario: A design review meeting at a life insurer evaluating a proposed robust risk module for joint life insurance products before it is folded into the quarterly pricing and capital workflow. The proposal adapts recent research on dependence uncertainty by using concordance-based monotonicity results and linear-program bounds for mean, Value-at-Risk, and Expected Shortfall around a reference copula. The context is that the company has sparse dependent-life experience data for spouse and business-partner policies, and the existing dependence stress is viewed as too coarse for product pricing and second-line model challenge. The agenda is to review whether the design is suitable for the current joint-life portfolio, whether the assumptions and implementation boundaries are acceptable for governance, and what modifications are needed before sign-off. The expected outcome is a decision on whether to approve the design in principle for the next model release, with a short list of follow-up changes and owners.

members.name: Elena Chen
members.role: Lead Pricing Actuary, Longevity & Protection Solutions
members.expertise: Joint-life product pricing, copula-based dependence modeling, capital impact translation for life insurance portfolios
members.background: Elena leads the actuarial design work for retail protection products and has been translating recent academic results into practical pricing tools for the insurer's joint-life term, whole-life, and last-survivor products.
members.private_state: She wants the design review to end with conditional approval so her team can include the module in the next quarterly pricing refresh; she is especially concerned about keeping the implementation narrow enough that the theorem-backed monotonicity results remain valid and the runtime stays manageable.
hidden_assumptions: When people say the 'joint-life block,' they mean the subset of standard first-to-die and last-survivor contracts with payoff structures covered by the monotonicity result, not every policy with two insured lives.
The '2019 dependence study' refers to the internally relabeled experience-study framework that was rebuilt and cleaned over 2019-2023, not the original archived 2019 governance package.
A norm-ball around the reference copula should be applied separately within each pricing cell because the optimization is solved cell-by-cell and then aggregated.
If the LP bounds are numerically reproducible on the representative age grid and benchmark cases, that is enough to call the design 'stable' for review purposes.

members.name: David Morales
members.role: Director of Model Risk & Product Governance
members.expertise: Model validation, governance standards, actuarial control frameworks, approval of pricing and capital methodologies
members.background: David oversees second-line review for actuarial models used in pricing and reserving, with a focus on ensuring methods align with approved documentation, governance definitions, and enterprise capital reporting conventions.
members.private_state: He wants to avoid approving a design that later requires a governance exception or creates unexplained capital volatility in quarterly committee reporting; he is willing to support the proposal if it fits existing approval boundaries and does not expand validation scope unexpectedly.
hidden_assumptions: When a design is presented for the 'joint-life block,' it should cover all products grouped under the joint-life governance umbrella, including rider-based survivor benefits that are reported with that block.
The '2019 dependence study' means the last formally approved study artifact on file, because governance references approved versions rather than internal recalibrations.
A norm-ball around the reference copula is a single model-level uncertainty allowance, so the radius should be set once at portfolio level for consistency and auditability.
A design is only 'stable' if ordinary quarterly data updates do not cause material movement in reported capital or pricing loadings.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the joint-life block
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both discuss applying the method to the 'joint-life block' and 'standard joint-life products.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means only first-to-die, second-death, and last-survivor contracts whose payoff structures fall within the theorem-backed contract class for monotonicity under concordance order.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the whole governance bucket of joint-life business, including bundled survivor-income riders and reversionary-annuity features reported with joint-life products.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both sides hear familiar portfolio shorthand and assume the product taxonomy is shared; because neither wants to derail the review into product inventory details, the phrase 'joint-life block' passes as sufficiently precise.

misalignment_points.topic: Which 2019 dependence study is the reference
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both refer to calibrating around the '2019 dependence study' or the '2019 reference copula.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of her team's cleaned and updated calibration framework, internally nicknamed the '2019 study' because it originated from that project, with spouse-age adjustments and exclusions for incomplete joint records.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the archived, formally approved 2019 study package held in model governance, based on the original policyholder-pair extract and older data-cleaning rules.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The label is institutional shorthand used by both teams, and each assumes there is only one salient '2019 study'; since the review focuses on design rather than document control, the specific artifact is never named.

misalignment_points.topic: How the uncertainty radius is applied
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to use a 'norm-ball around the reference copula with epsilon set by governance.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes epsilon is applied separately within each pricing segment such as age-band and smoker-status cells, because the LPs are solved per segment and then rolled up.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes epsilon is one portfolio-level radius applied globally to the model's dependence specification, because governance tolerances are set once per approved model component.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: At a surface level both are endorsing the same mathematical idea and the same symbol epsilon; the difference lies in where the radius attaches in the workflow, which feels like an implementation detail rather than something requiring explicit discussion.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both say the bounds need to be 'stable' and 'ready for sign-off.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the optimization returns reproducible bound estimates within a tight numerical tolerance on the representative test grid and does not show solver pathologies.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the resulting pricing loads and capital numbers should not move materially under routine quarterly refreshes or small experience changes.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In design reviews, 'stable' is a universally positive term that usually goes unchallenged; each participant silently maps it to the kind of stability most relevant to their own function.
